item.title: Nothing Particularly Remarkable
item.author: raams.karthik@gmail.com (Karthik Ganeshram)
item.description:
I was talking to someone recently about photography, and we found ourselves agreeing that neither of us necessarily takes photographs to look back at them.

Which is funny, considering the number of pictures sitting in my camera roll that I’ll probably never open again.

I’ve always enjoyed walking around with no particular destination, especially when visiting a new city. And somewhere along the way, I’ve started taking more photographs of the seemingly unremarkable things I come across. A peculiar building, an interesting reflection, or a street that looks a little different in the afternoon light.

But I’ve been wondering what makes me stop and take a photograph in the first place.

Sometimes it’s the light, an interesting composition, or a detail I hadn’t noticed before. Other times, I couldn’t really tell you why. Something just caught my eye.

I could walk down the same street a hundred times and only notice something interesting on the hundred-and-first. Someone else might walk alongside me and notice something entirely different.

I quite like that thought. The same surroundings, but a slightly different experience depending on who’s looking.

And maybe that’s what I enjoy about sharing these little photographs too. It’s not necessarily about showing someone something spectacular. Sometimes it’s just a way of saying, “Here’s something that caught my eye today.”

They might not find it particularly remarkable, and that’s perfectly fine.

I probably won’t look at half these photographs again anyway. But I do enjoy that taking them makes me pay a little more attention to the world around me.

And occasionally, I get to see what caught someone else’s eye too.

item.title: Saaptiya? And Other Little Things
item.author: raams.karthik@gmail.com (Karthik Ganeshram)
item.description:
I’ve been back in Chennai for a couple of weeks now, and one of the things I’ve enjoyed is hearing the familiar saaptiya? (Have you eaten?) again. It’s a question I’ve heard countless times growing up, from family, relatives, and just about anyone who knows me.

It’s a funny question when you think about it. Sometimes the person asking doesn’t particularly need an answer. It’s a greeting, a check-in, and an expression of care, all wrapped into one small question. Growing up, it was simply part of everyday life, along with the insistence that anyone visiting should have something to eat, even if they’d already said no.

I never gave these things much thought growing up. At a wedding recently, I found myself explaining some of these everyday expressions and gestures to the guests from the bride’s side, who were Australian. Trying to put them into words made me notice how many had followed me into life away from Chennai.

I love cooking for people. Not necessarily hosting elaborate dinner parties, but inviting a friend or two over and making something I think they’ll enjoy. Sometimes that’s a biryani, other times an elaborate dessert I’ve spent far too much time experimenting with. I enjoy the process, but more than anything, I enjoy sharing the result.

A little while ago, I baked four different kinds of cookies for the birthday of a barista at my regular café in Rotterdam. It was a small gesture for someone who’d become a familiar part of my mornings. I didn’t have to do it, of course, but I wanted to.

Perhaps that’s my own version of saaptiya? It’s not always about the food. Sometimes making something for someone is simply a way of saying that you appreciate them.

Another thing I’ve noticed being back in Chennai is how naturally the word anna slips into conversations. Literally meaning “elder brother,” it’s used to address everyone from a shopkeeper to an auto driver. When I tell an auto driver where I’m going, anna comes out before the destination. We don’t know each other’s names, but the conversation already feels a little less anonymous.

In Rotterdam, I’ve come to appreciate a similar kind of familiarity in my everyday routines. There’s my regular café, where a quick stop for coffee can turn into a conversation with the barista, familiar faces at the gym, and people I regularly meet through cycling. These aren’t necessarily close friendships, nor do they need to be. But they make the city feel a little more like home.

Then there’s poitu varen, roughly translating to “I’ll go and come back.” It’s a common way of saying goodbye in Tamil, and I’ve always liked that it doesn’t quite sound like an ending.

I’ve noticed that I instinctively say “see you” or “see you soon” rather than “goodbye.” I can’t say for certain that one comes from the other, but I enjoy the similarity. There’s something nice about leaving with the possibility of another meeting, even if you don’t know when that might be.

After years on the West Coast of the United States and in Rotterdam, being back in Chennai has made me notice what I carried away: a question about food, a familiar word for a stranger, a way of leaving that makes room for another hello. None of these felt like lessons growing up. They were simply part of the day, and now I find them in the life I’ve built elsewhere.

Poitu varen.

item.title: What we push against
item.author: raams.karthik@gmail.com (Karthik Ganeshram)
item.description:
While I was listening to a podcast recently, I heard someone describe the idea that freedom enables creativity as a myth. It stayed with me. Perhaps because I had recently been hearing a similar idea about AI: that by removing the barriers to creation, it will give more people the freedom to express their creativity.

I think that is true, to an extent.

Freedom can absolutely enable creativity. Having the time, space, tools, and ability to pursue an idea matters. Removing unnecessary barriers can allow people to create things they otherwise might never have been able to.

But I am not convinced that freedom alone is enough.

When I have too many options, I often become indecisive. When I am free to do anything, it can become surprisingly easy to do nothing.

A problem gives you something to solve. A deadline gives you a reason to act. A limitation gives you something to work around. In each case, there is something to push against.

You cannot really move forward by pushing against nothing. Movement requires resistance. Maybe creativity is similar. Maybe we need something to respond to - Something to solve, Something to overcome, Something to push against.

This is where I find myself slightly sceptical of the idea that removing all barriers will automatically make people more creative. If everything is possible, choosing what to do can become its own problem.

When everything is possible, nothing is necessary.

I realise this may be a privileged thing to think about. I am fortunate enough to have a reasonable amount of freedom in my life. I have the luxury of wondering whether too much freedom can sometimes make it harder to create.

So this is not really an argument against freedom. I think freedom gives creativity space but I also think constraints give it direction. Maybe the most fertile ground for creativity is somewhere between the two: enough freedom to explore, but enough resistance to make exploration necessary.

I am still thinking about it.

But I am increasingly convinced that creativity does not come from freedom alone. Sometimes, the thing that forces us to create is the thing that gives us something to push against.

item.title: Coffee, Pastries, and the Joy in the Little Things
item.author: raams.karthik@gmail.com (Karthik Ganeshram)
item.description:
I’ve always had a sweet tooth. But this year, that small craving has grown into something much bigger, a lens through which I’ve been noticing joy in unexpected, everyday moments.

It all started back in March while traveling. In Porto with a friend, we turned bakery-hopping into a game: stopping at nearly every bakery we passed and tasting pastéis de nata and other treats. When I got home, I couldn’t stop thinking about them, so I decided to bake pastéis de nata from scratch. They weren’t perfect, but the process reminded me that small efforts like whisking custard or folding pastry can bring a lot of satisfaction, even if the result isn’t flawless.

A few weeks later, I was in Barcelona with a coworker, continuing the tradition of wandering into bakeries. By the end of the trip, it was clear that I wasn’t just enjoying pastries, I was savoring the simple, grounding pleasure of experiencing them fully, and it always felt even better with a good cup of coffee in hand.

Back in Rotterdam, this curiosity for small joys found its rhythm. At first, pastries and coffee were simply a reward for finishing a morning run - a small, deliberate indulgence that made early mornings feel lighter. Soon I began sharing them with a friend, turning it into a weekly ritual: picking up pastries and meeting to catch up over breakfast before work. Those quiet mornings, sipping coffee and savoring something sweet, became one of my favorite parts of the week.

During the summer, all the biking around Rotterdam made these small pleasures feel earned. My friends and I would detour to little cafés for coffee and pastries. And somewhere along the way, I also fell in love with solitary mornings: waking up early, stepping out while the city is still quiet, grabbing a fresh cup of coffee, and walking along the Maas. Sitting by the bridge or wandering along the water with that warm drink, I realized that these small, intentional moments with a coffee in hand and the city still asleep can feel profoundly joyful.

As for favorites: Ripsnorter and Cafecito for coffee; Le Petit Jean, my regular breakfast spot with a friend; Lila Bakery for its Eastern European cakes. My only frustration used to be that most bakeries in Rotterdam don’t open before 8 a.m. By then I’d already been up, ready for my treat with my nose pressed up against the windows waiting for the shutters to open. But discovering that the Albert Heijn next to my house has fresh pastéis de nata at 7 a.m., paired with a strong cup of coffee, felt like a small victory. A reminder that joy can be found in tiny, everyday discoveries.

Later in the year, my love for pastries and coffee followed me on trips abroad. In July, a short vacation in Copenhagen was spent with quiet mornings wandering the city with Danish pastries and café lattés, and in late September, a vacation in Nice and Paris with coworkers before an offsite continued the streak with croissants, éclairs, and warm cafés. Those mornings in Copenhagen, Nice, and Paris reinforced a lesson I had been learning all year: delight isn’t reserved for big moments or grand adventures. It can be found in small, intentional acts, pausing to savor a pastry, sipping coffee slowly while the city wakes, or noticing the little rituals that make ordinary days richer.

What began as a joke in Portugal has become a rhythm that follows me everywhere: runs that end with pastries, breakfasts with friends, bike rides that detour for coffee, and quiet walks with a warm cup in hand. Whether I’m in Rotterdam, Paris, or elsewhere, I’ve realized that joy often hides in the little things, the first sip of morning coffee, the flaky edge of a croissant, the stillness of a city before it wakes up.

Now that fall is here, I’m excited to keep the ritual alive: to wake up early, explore quiet streets, and let soft, dark mornings remind me that life’s sweetness often comes in small, intentional moments. Coffee and pastries, in their simplicity, have shown me that joy doesn’t always arrive in grand gestures; it often lives quietly, in cups, crumbs, and the deliberate act of slowing down.
